title: Boldfit raises ₹400 crore Series B led by Bharat Value Fund
excerpt: Bengaluru fitness brand Boldfit raised over ₹400 crore from Bharat Value Fund and Bessemer to open stores, scale manufacturing and pursue acquisitions.
content:
Boldfit, the Bengaluru fitness and sportswear brand, has raised more than ₹400 crore (about $42 million) in a Series B round led by Bharat Value Fund, the company said on 12 October 2026, according to Business Today. The money is meant to take a brand that grew up selling online into physical stores across India, while it scales manufacturing and looks for acquisitions.

No valuation was disclosed. Existing investor Bessemer Venture Partners also put money into the round.

Key takeaways

  • Boldfit raised over ₹400 crore in a Series B led by Bharat Value Fund, with Bessemer Venture Partners participating. A crore is 10 million rupees.
  • The plan for the money: a nationwide retail footprint, more manufacturing, new products and selective acquisitions.
  • Together with its ₹110 crore Series A, the disclosed rounds add up to more than ₹510 crore. Its previous round was ₹110 crore from Bessemer in November 2024.
  • The deal is being described as Bharat Value Fund's largest consumer-sector investment so far, according to Business Today.

The round: who invested and how much

Bharat Value Fund led the Series B. It is a Category II alternative investment fund (AIF), a SEBI-regulated pool that typically backs unlisted companies, and it is managed by The Wealth Company Alternates, part of the Pantomath Group, as DealStreetAsia reported. DealStreetAsia put the fund's cheque at about ₹400 crore ($41.8 million), while the company and other outlets describe the round as "over" ₹400 crore. Bessemer Venture Partners, which led Boldfit's previous round, came back in, according to Entrepreneur India.

Avendus Capital acted as the exclusive financial adviser to Boldfit and its shareholders. Neither side disclosed the valuation, the stake the fund bought, or how much of the round was new capital versus shares bought from earlier backers.

The deal is Bharat Value Fund's fourth sizeable bet in the past 12 months, after Zetwerk Manufacturing, Amnex Infotechnologies and Big Mishra, Business Today reported. When its third fund reached a first close of ₹1,250 crore in January 2025, the manager said it was aiming for ₹2,500 crore and wanted mid-sized, fast-growing companies with revenue of ₹300–1,000 crore, with an eye on exits through IPOs within roughly three years, according to Inc42. That profile, a pre-IPO investor, hints at where Boldfit may be heading, though neither party has said anything about a listing.

Founder and CEO Pallav Bihani said the company is building "a deeply integrated sports business", according to BestMediaInfo. Madhu Lunawat of The Wealth Company said the investment reflects the fund's conviction in Boldfit's growth potential.

What Boldfit sells

Boldfit was founded in 2018 by Pallav Bihani and Aasshna Guptaa, according to Entrackr. It started as a direct-to-consumer (D2C) brand, meaning it sells under its own name online rather than through distributors, and its range now covers performance sportswear, athletic footwear, sports equipment and fitness accessories such as yoga mats, gym gear and supplements. In 2024 it listed more than 400 products, pitched at affordable price points, as Inc42 reported.

It sells through online marketplaces, quick-commerce apps and its own website, according to SiliconIndia. The company says it serves more than 2 crore (20 million) customers a year and has grown at a compound annual rate of over 80% across the last three years. Both figures are the company's own and have not been independently verified.

Celebrity backing has been part of the pitch. Cricketer KL Rahul invested in July 2024 and is the brand ambassador, and tennis player Sania Mirza is also an investor, according to Business Today.

What the published financials show

Boldfit is run by Bling Brands Private Limited, which is unlisted. Inc42's company database lists standalone total revenue of ₹140 crore and a profit after tax of ₹16.8 crore for FY24 (April 2023 to March 2024), with total expenses of ₹116.3 crore, according to Inc42. That would make Boldfit one of the few Indian D2C brands of its size reporting a profit. Lunawat described the business as anchored by profitability, as Entrepreneur India reported.

A caution: published reports do not agree on which fiscal year some of these figures belong to, and we did not find audited FY25 numbers in the coverage we checked. We have left out any figure we could not tie to a named source, and the company did not disclose revenue alongside this round.

Where the money goes

Boldfit has given four uses for the capital, according to DealStreetAsia and Business Today:

  • Retail stores across India. Building a nationwide offline presence to sit alongside its online business. It has not said how many stores it plans.
  • Manufacturing. Scaling up its manufacturing capabilities.
  • Product development. New products in sportswear, footwear and equipment.
  • Acquisitions. Selective deals to enter new categories or deepen existing ones.

The move offline is not new thinking. When Boldfit raised its Series A in November 2024, it said it would open offline stores within 12 to 18 months and expand into the Middle East, according to Entrackr. This round pays for that plan on a much larger scale.

The Indian fitness and D2C context

India's government has pushed fitness as a public cause since the Prime Minister launched the Fit India Movement on National Sports Day, 29 August 2019, according to the Press Information Bureau. Demand for home workout gear, running shoes and gym accessories has created space for value-priced Indian brands next to global names.

The market numbers in circulation are mostly estimates. Boldfit's 2024 funding coverage cited a figure of $20 billion for India's fitness market in 2023, projected to reach $32 billion by 2028, according to Entrackr. Treat that as an industry projection rather than a measured figure.

The bigger story is the D2C playbook. Brands that grew on marketplaces often hit a ceiling when ad costs rise and platform fees bite. Physical stores help with brand trust, let shoppers try on shoes and clothing, and reach buyers who still prefer offline shopping, but they also add rent, staff and inventory risk. Boldfit is betting its reported profitability gives it room to absorb those costs.

Why it matters

A ₹400 crore Series B is large for an Indian consumer brand, and the investor mix is telling. A pre-IPO fund leading, with a growth-stage VC following on, suggests backers see Boldfit moving from a fast-growing online seller towards a scaled, multi-channel company. The test now is execution: opening stores profitably, running factories well, and integrating any acquisitions without losing the margins that made it attractive. FAQ

How much did Boldfit raise in its Series B?

More than ₹400 crore, about $42 million, announced on 12 October 2026. Bharat Value Fund led and Bessemer Venture Partners participated.

Who owns Boldfit?

Boldfit is run by Bling Brands Private Limited, founded by Pallav Bihani and Aasshna Guptaa. Investors include Bharat Value Fund, Bessemer Venture Partners, KL Rahul and Sania Mirza. Shareholding percentages have not been published.

What is Boldfit's valuation?

It was not disclosed for this round, and we do not estimate it.

Is Boldfit profitable?

Inc42's company database lists a profit after tax of ₹16.8 crore on ₹140 crore of revenue for FY24. Later audited figures were not available in the coverage we checked.

What is Bharat Value Fund?

A Category II AIF managed by The Wealth Company Alternates, part of the Pantomath Group. It focuses on mid-sized companies preparing for public listing.
